entries.question: How many of Bebai's offspring returned from Babylon?
entries.summary: Ezra 2:11 reports 623 children of Bebai returned from Babylon. Nehemiah 7:16 gives 628 for the same family in the same returnee list. Five-person discrepancy in a roster that both texts claim to be reproducing from the same source document.
entries.commentary:
This is another data point in the Ezra 2 versus Nehemiah 7 divergence problem, and it deserves to be treated as part of the same pattern rather than as a standalone puzzle. The two lists are not independent — Nehemiah 7:5 is explicit that the chapter is a copy of the original returnee registry. Yet across roughly two dozen family entries, the numbers disagree more than half the time. That is a transmission problem.

The standard harmonization, which goes back at least to Keil-Delitzsch in the nineteenth century, is that one list was taken at a different point in time than the other — people died, people changed their minds, people had children. That sounds tidy until you actually run the math. The Ezra and Nehemiah totals do not just drift in one direction; some families gain people and other families lose people. If this were genuine attrition or growth, you would expect some directional pattern. You don't get one. You get the random walk you would expect from scribes miscopying numerals.

Williamson in his WBC volume and Blenkinsopp in his OTL volume both point to the fact that 1 Esdras 5 — a Greek text reproducing essentially the same list — sometimes agrees with Ezra against Nehemiah, sometimes with Nehemiah against Ezra, and sometimes gives a third number entirely. For Bebai specifically, 1 Esdras 5:13 reads 623 (agreeing with Ezra against Nehemiah's 628), which makes Nehemiah the likely site of the corruption. That kind of two-against-one alignment is exactly how textual critics triangulate the original reading. Hebrew scribes were generally careful, but numerical material is notoriously the first thing to drift, because numbers carry no semantic redundancy — there is nothing in the sentence around the number to help a scribe catch a slip.

The apologist needs both numbers to be correct, because both books claim divine origin and both claim to be reproducing the same source. The critical scholar just needs the texts to be human documents that drifted in transmission, which is exactly what the manuscript evidence shows. One of those positions has a mechanism. The other has a problem.

answers.answer_explanation: The children of Bebai, six hundred twenty and three. Ezra 2:11
The children of Bebai, six hundred twenty and eight. Nehemiah 7:16

commentary_out.commentary:
The Bebai entry is one node in a systemic problem: across roughly two dozen family entries in the parallel rosters of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, the totals disagree in more than half the cases. Ezra 2:11 gives 623 children of Bebai; Nehemiah 7:16 gives 628 — a five-person gap. Crucially, the two lists are not independent. Nehemiah 7:5 states that the chapter reproduces "the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first," so both texts depend on one underlying register (the Golah list). The disagreements are therefore disagreements within a single document's transmission history, which reframes the whole question from "two events" to "two copies."

The most durable harmonization, traceable at least to Keil and Delitzsch in the nineteenth century and repeated in much conservative literature since, holds that the two lists were taken at different moments — that deaths, defections, late arrivals, and births in the interval account for the divergences. The proposal is tidy until tested against the data. If genuine attrition or growth were the cause, the discrepancies should trend in a consistent direction or at least correlate with something. They do not. Some families gain people in Nehemiah relative to Ezra; others lose people; the magnitudes range from one to over a thousand with no demographic logic linking them. That is the profile of a random walk produced by independent copying errors, not of a population changing between two reliable censuses. The time-snapshot theory also has to be invoked dozens of times in a single chapter, and it never explains why Nehemiah, who claims to be reproducing an older document, would silently substitute later figures for the ones in his source.

The versional evidence sharpens the diagnosis. 1 Esdras 5 reproduces essentially the same list in Greek and functions as a third, partly independent witness. In the standard versification of 1 Esdras 5:13, the sons of Bebai are given as 623 — agreeing with Ezra against Nehemiah's 628. That two-against-one alignment is precisely how textual critics triangulate an archetype: when two witnesses converge and a third diverges, the divergent reading is the more likely corruption — here pointing to Nehemiah 7:16 as the site of the slip. The caveat worth stating plainly is that 1 Esdras's own numerals are not perfectly stable across its manuscript streams, so the alignment is a strong indicator rather than a closed case. Williamson in WBC 16 and Blenkinsopp in the OTL volume both treat these numerical divergences as transmissional, and Sara Japhet's studies of the restoration period reach the same conclusion: the lists are paired copies, not paired censuses.

The underlying mechanism is well understood. Hebrew numerical material is the most error-prone category in any manuscript, because numbers carry no semantic redundancy. The words around a misread verb or name constrain the possible readings and let a careful scribe catch a slip; a misread number is invisible to such checks. Whether the figures were copied from a damaged exemplar or taken by dictation, the units and tens positions are exactly where transmission fails first, a pattern Tov documents across the canon and which recurs in the Kings-versus-Chronicles totals and the Genesis genealogies across MT, LXX, and the Samaritan Pentateuch.

The apologetic position requires both numbers to be original and correct, since both books are held to be inspired and both claim the same source. The critical position requires only that these be human documents whose numerals drifted in copying — which is what the three-witness evidence directly shows. One account supplies a mechanism that fits the data; the other supplies a harmonization that the data contradict. Verdict: genuine discrepancy, scribal corruption, with 1 Esdras pointing to Nehemiah as the corrupt witness.

entries.question: How many of Azgad's offspring returned from Babylon?
entries.summary: Ezra 2:12 counts 1,222 returnees from the family of Azgad. Nehemiah 7:17 gives 2,322 for the same family in the same roster. This is not a five-person rounding error — the two numbers differ by 1,100 people.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the more spectacular numerical disagreements in the Ezra/Nehemiah parallel and it is exactly the kind of case where the apologist's 'maybe people died between censuses' explanation completely falls apart. The discrepancy is 1,100 people in a single family. You do not lose or gain a thousand people from one family entry through normal demographic drift between two near-contemporary records of the same event.

What you do get is a perfectly recognizable scribal mechanism. In Hebrew, the numbers 'one thousand' (eleph) and 'two thousand' (alpayim) are visually close, and the units and hundreds positions can be confused in early square-script manuscripts. 1 Esdras 5:13 — an independent Greek transmission of the same list — gives 1,322 in the main text (close to Ezra's 1,222) with variant readings of 3,222 and 3,622 in some witnesses, showing that the textual tradition was unstable across multiple streams. This is not a 'God said it twice with a different emphasis' situation. This is a numerical roster that scribes could not keep stable.

Williamson in WBC 16 notes that the Azgad numbers in particular are 'almost certainly corrupt' in at least one of the two Hebrew witnesses, and Blenkinsopp concurs. Critical scholarship has largely stopped trying to defend the integrity of these numbers and treats them as a textbook case of why we cannot speak of a single, stable, perfectly preserved Hebrew text. The numbers in Kings versus Chronicles, the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 across MT/LXX/SP, and these Ezra/Nehemiah totals all show the same pattern: numerical data is exactly where transmission fails.

The apologetic move of choice — 'one is a count from before the journey, the other after' — does not work for a discrepancy this large. You would need a thousand-person catastrophe localized to a single family while every other family stays stable or grows. There is no such mechanism in the text. The honest read is that we have a corrupted number somewhere in the transmission, and inerrancy as classically formulated does not survive that admission.

The children of Azgad, one thousand two hundred twenty and
				          two. Ezra 2:12

The children of Azgad, two thousand three hundred twenty
				          and two. Nehemiah 7:17

commentary_out.commentary:
The Azgad entry is the most dramatic of the Ezra 2 / Nehemiah 7 numerical disagreements and the clearest test of the standard harmonizations. Ezra 2:12 counts 1,222 returnees from the family of Azgad; Nehemiah 7:17 gives 2,322 — a gap of 1,100 people in a single family. As with every other entry in these parallel rosters, the two lists are not independent records: Nehemiah 7:5 frames the whole chapter as a copy of "the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first." One source document, two transmissions, two wildly different figures for the same household.

The favored apologetic reconciliation — that one figure counts the family before the journey and the other after, with the difference absorbed by deaths, defections, or late arrivals — collapses here on arithmetic alone. A swing of 1,100 people would require either a catastrophe or an influx localized to one family while the surrounding entries remain stable or move by single and double digits. No such mechanism exists in the text, and nothing in the narrative records a localized demographic event of that scale. The discrepancy is far too large for any plausible attrition-or-growth story.

What the data fit instead is a recognizable scribal mechanism. In the Masoretic tradition these totals are written out as words, and the terms for "one thousand" (eleph) and "two thousand" (alpayim) are close enough that confusion in the thousands position is an easy slip, while the hundreds digit can drift independently. The versional witness confirms the instability: in the standard versification of 1 Esdras 5:13, the sons of Azgad are given as 1,322, close to Ezra's 1,222 and a third figure distinct from Nehemiah's 2,322. A datum that surfaces in the witnesses as 1,222, 1,322, and 2,322 has plainly not been transmitted stably; it has fractured across the manuscript streams, and 1 Esdras's own numerals are themselves not uniform across its copies. Williamson notes that the Azgad numbers are almost certainly corrupt in at least one of the two Hebrew witnesses, and Blenkinsopp concurs.

This is not an isolated curiosity. Numerical corruption of exactly this kind recurs across the Hebrew Bible: the differing army and tribute totals between Samuel-Kings and Chronicles, and the patriarchal ages of Genesis 5 and 11 diverging across MT, LXX, and the Samaritan Pentateuch. The regnal formula of 1 Samuel 13:1 — where the MT literally reads that Saul was "a year old when he began to reign" and reigned "two years," with the larger figure simply missing — belongs to the same family of problems, though it is a case of lost or never-preserved numerical text rather than a clean miscopied digit. Emanuel Tov treats numerals as the category most exposed to transmission error precisely because they lack the semantic redundancy that lets a scribe catch a mistake in ordinary prose. Loring Batten's ICC volume and Zipora Talshir's study of 1 Esdras both document how the restoration-period lists were copied and recopied with the numbers drifting in each stream.

The inerrantist needs both figures to be original and correct, but the magnitude of the Azgad gap leaves no room for a perspectival or chronological dodge — the text claims one source, and a single family does not gain or shed a thousand people between two near-contemporary copies of the same register. Critical scholarship has largely abandoned the defense of these figures and reads them as a textbook demonstration that no single, perfectly preserved Hebrew text underlies the witnesses we possess. Verdict: genuine discrepancy, certain numeral corruption in transmission.

entries.question: How many of Adonikam's offspring returned from Babylon?
entries.summary: Ezra 2:13 has 666 sons of Adonikam returning from Babylon. Nehemiah 7:18, copying the same registry, gives 667. A single-digit discrepancy in a number that the biblical text says is precise to the individual.
entries.commentary:
On a percentage basis this is the smallest of the Ezra/Nehemiah discrepancies in the family rolls, and the apologist will of course point to that — one person, what's the big deal. The point is not the size of the gap. The point is that there is a gap at all in a list that both books claim to be transmitting from a common source document. Nehemiah 7:5 explicitly frames the chapter as a reproduction of 'the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first.' One source, two copies, two different numbers.

The traditional harmonization here is that someone died on the road or someone joined late, and the two figures reflect two different snapshots in time. Keil-Delitzsch leaned on this in the nineteenth century and Archer continues it in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties. The problem with the time-snapshot defense is that it has to be deployed dozens of times across the chapter, with the numbers drifting in both directions, and it never explains why Nehemiah — who is reproducing an earlier document — would have updated the numbers to reflect later demographics rather than just copying the source. The text does not claim to be updating. It claims to be transmitting.

Williamson, Blenkinsopp, and Klein all read these single-digit discrepancies as ordinary scribal slips in numerical transmission. Hebrew numbers written out as words are still vulnerable when a scribe is working from a damaged exemplar or from dictation, and the units position is the most error-prone slot in any numeral. The 666/667 split is almost certainly one of those slips, not a theological signal and not a demographic event.

The interesting thing about the 666 figure is its later afterlife — popular apocalyptic readers from the medieval period through modern dispensationalists have occasionally read Adonikam's number as somehow significant given Revelation 13:18. That is a fun coincidence and nothing more, since 1 Esdras 5:14 reads 667 (agreeing with Nehemiah against Ezra) and the wider list shows the same kind of numerical instability across MT, LXX, and the 1 Esdras tradition. Coincidence theology built on a textually unstable number is a house built on sand.

answers.answer_explanation: The children of Adonikam, six hundred sixty and six. Ezra 2:13
The children of Adonikam, six hundred threescore and seven. Nehemiah 7:18

commentary_out.commentary:
On a percentage basis the Adonikam entry is the smallest of the Ezra 2 / Nehemiah 7 family discrepancies: Ezra 2:13 reads 666, Nehemiah 7:18 reads 667 — a difference of one person. The triviality of the gap is exactly what makes it instructive. The issue is not magnitude but the existence of any disagreement at all in a list that both books claim to transmit from a single source. Nehemiah 7:5 explicitly frames the chapter as a reproduction of "the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first." One register, two copies, two totals that fail to match even by a single unit.

The traditional harmonization, deployed by Keil and Delitzsch in the nineteenth century and carried forward by Gleason Archer, holds that the two figures are snapshots taken at different times — one person died on the road, or one joined late, and the lists record different moments. The defense has two structural weaknesses. First, it must be invoked dozens of times across the chapter, with the numbers drifting in both directions, which strains any single demographic explanation past credibility. Second, and decisively, it conflicts with Nehemiah's own claim. Nehemiah does not present himself as updating the figures to reflect later demographics; he presents himself as transmitting an older document. A copyist reproducing a register does not silently re-poll the population. The time-snapshot theory thus supplies a story the text itself does not authorize.

The controlling mechanism is far simpler. Single-unit divergences are the classic fingerprint of scribal slips in the units position of a numeral, the most error-prone slot in any number because it carries no semantic constraint. Even where numbers are written out as words, a scribe working from a damaged exemplar or from dictation can drop or add a unit without any contextual check to catch it. The versional evidence here aligns 1 Esdras with Nehemiah rather than Ezra: in the standard versification of 1 Esdras 5:14, the sons of Adonikam are given as 667, matching Nehemiah's figure against Ezra's 666, while the broader list shows the same instability across MT, LXX, and the 1 Esdras tradition that characterizes every entry in these parallel rolls. The caveat from the other entries holds — 1 Esdras's own numerals are not uniform across its copies — so the alignment is an indicator, not a proof, of which side carries the slip. Williamson, Blenkinsopp, and Klein all classify these single-digit divergences as ordinary transmissional noise rather than theological signal or demographic record.

The figure 666 occasionally gets pulled into popular numerology, and it is worth addressing only to set it aside. Because Ezra 2:13 reads 666, some popular writing has noted the coincidence with the "number of the beast" in Revelation 13:18. There is no documented interpretive tradition tying the two together; it is a passing observation, not an exegetical lineage. And it is coincidence and nothing more: the Greek apocalyptic figure of Revelation has no literary or historical relationship to a Persian-period family roster, and the very instability of the datum — appearing as 666 in Ezra and 667 in both Nehemiah and 1 Esdras — undercuts any claim that the precise value carries hidden significance. A theology built on a textually unstable number is built on sand.

For the inerrantist even a one-person gap is a problem in principle, because the doctrine asserts precision to the individual and both books claim the same source. The critical reading needs only a human document copied imperfectly, which is exactly what the three-witness evidence shows. Verdict: genuine discrepancy, minor scribal slip in the units position, with 1 Esdras aligning the variant with Nehemiah.

entries.question: How much gold, silver, and clothing did the people give?
entries.summary: Ezra 2:69 records the returnees' contribution to the temple treasury as 61,000 drams of gold, 5,000 pounds of silver, and 100 priests' garments. Nehemiah 7:72, transmitting the same registry, gives 20,000 drams of gold, 2,000 pounds of silver, and 67 priests' garments. Three separate categories of donation, three separate disagreements, in a single ledger entry that both texts claim to be reproducing from a common source.
entries.commentary:
This is the climactic divergence in the Ezra 2 / Nehemiah 7 parallel and it cannot be rescued by any of the standard harmonizations. The discrepancies in the family rosters might be argued away one by one by appeal to scribal slips or demographic updates, but the donation ledger disagrees across three separate categories simultaneously — gold, silver, and priestly garments — and the disagreements are large in every category. Sixty-one thousand drams versus twenty thousand. Five thousand pounds versus two thousand. One hundred garments versus sixty-seven.

The apologetic playbook here gets really creative. One move is to argue that Ezra 2 records the total contribution while Nehemiah 7 records only the contribution of the laity, with the priests and Levites contributing separately and Nehemiah omitting their share. This is essentially the position taken by Archer in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties. The problem is that the text of Nehemiah 7:70-72 actually does break down the contributions by donor category (the governor, the heads of the fathers, and the rest of the people) and the sum of those breakdowns still does not produce the Ezra 2 total. So the rescue requires further patching.

Williamson in WBC 16 reads this as one of the clearest cases of full-blown editorial intervention in one of the two transmissions. The Nehemiah 7 ledger has been reorganized to break down the donations by donor category, and in the process the numbers have either been altered, corrupted, or were never the same as Ezra 2 to begin with. Blenkinsopp concurs and adds that the dram counts in particular are suspect because the unit of measurement (the daric) is anachronistic to the period of the original return, which suggests that at least one of the editors has updated the figures to reflect a later currency standard. That kind of editorial updating is exactly what we would expect from human transmission and exactly what we would not expect from divinely inspired identical reproduction.

The critical verdict here is that the donation ledger is the strongest single case in the entire chapter for editorial intervention in transmission. The numbers are not just numerically different — they are categorically restructured in ways that no demographic-update theory can absorb. The apologist needs all three totals in all three categories to be simultaneously correct. The critical scholar just needs editorial reorganization across two centuries of transmission. One position has a mechanism that fits the evidence. The other is paying compound tolls. Take your pick.

commentary_out.commentary:
The donation ledger is the climactic divergence of the Ezra 2 / Nehemiah 7 parallel, and it is the one entry that none of the standard harmonizations can absorb. Where the family and guild figures diverge in a single number that might be charged to a scribal slip, the treasury record disagrees across three independent categories at once, and by large margins in each. Ezra 2:69 records the returnees' gift as 61,000 darics (KJV "drams") of gold, 5,000 minas ("pounds") of silver, and 100 priestly garments. Nehemiah 7:72, in the clause covering "the rest of the people," gives 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver, and 67 priestly garments. Sixty-one thousand against twenty thousand; five thousand against two thousand; one hundred against sixty-seven. Three categories, three large disagreements.

The most serious harmonization is the donor-stratification argument, advanced in its strongest form by Gleason Archer in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties: Ezra 2:69 records the grand total of the community's gift, whereas Nehemiah 7:70-72 itemizes the donation by donor class and the figure in v. 72 is only the contribution of "the rest of the people," the laity, with the governor (the *Tirshatha*) and the heads of the ancestral houses giving separately in vv. 70-71; sum the strata and you recover Ezra's totals. This deserves a fair hearing, because Nehemiah 7 demonstrably does break the gift into donor categories where Ezra 2 gives a single lump. But the rescue fails on the arithmetic. Nehemiah's own itemized strata are: the governor (v. 70) gives 1,000 darics of gold, 50 basins, and 530 priestly garments; the heads of the ancestral houses (v. 71) give 20,000 darics of gold and 2,200 minas of silver; and the rest of the people (v. 72) give 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver, and 67 priestly garments. Add the gold and you get 41,000 darics — not Ezra 2:69's 61,000. The silver, leaving aside the governor's unstated share, totals 4,200 minas against Ezra's 5,000. The garments come to 597 against Ezra's flat 100. So the stratified figures do not reproduce Ezra's totals in any category; they overshoot the garments by nearly six-fold and undershoot the gold and silver. The stratification model therefore requires not one but a chain of further auxiliary assumptions — extra unrecorded donors, lost lines, scribal rounding — each unsupported by the text, to force agreement.

Williamson reads the ledger as the clearest case in the chapter of full editorial intervention in one of the two transmissions: the Nehemiah version has been restructured to distribute the gift across donor classes, and in that reworking the figures have been altered, corrupted, or were never identical to Ezra's to begin with. There is also a telling chronological point. The unit named, the daric, is a Persian gold coin that postdates the moment of the first return under Cyrus that the roster purports to date. (The popular derivation of the coin's name from Darius I is disputed among numismatists — some derive it from an Old Persian root for "gold" — but the dating point stands either way: the daric is not a Cyrus-era denomination.) Its presence signals that at least one editor has updated the monetary figures to a later currency standard — precisely the kind of secondary editorial reckoning that produces divergent numbers and that is incompatible with a model of inerrant identical reproduction.

The verdict is that this is the strongest single demonstration of editorial reworking in the whole roster. The numbers are not merely numerically different; the entry has been categorically restructured between the two recensions in a way no demographic- or scribal-slip theory can contain, and the anachronistic unit confirms secondary editorial activity. The apologist must make three totals in three categories simultaneously exact while supplying unstated arithmetic to bridge them; the critical scholar needs only editorial reorganization and currency updating across two centuries of transmission. Verdict: genuine and unharmonizable, the product of editorial intervention in the textual history.

commentary_out.change_summary: Roughly doubled the entry and then corrected the Nehemiah 7:70-72 donor breakdown, which had been garbled: stated the figures accurately (governor 1,000 darics gold / 50 basins / 530 garments; heads 20,000 darics gold / 2,200 minas silver; rest of the people 20,000 darics gold / 2,000 minas silver / 67 garments) and reworked the arithmetic rebuttal around the correct sums (gold strata total 41,000 vs. Ezra's 61,000; silver 4,200 vs. 5,000; garments 597 vs. 100). Qualified the daric point so the post-Cyrus dating carries the argument while flagging the Darius etymology as disputed, and stopped attributing the etymological claim specifically to Blenkinsopp. Corrected the earlier internal reference from 'Ezra 1 context' to the Nehemiah 7:70-72 breakdown. Retained Archer's laity-vs-priests harmonization steel-man and Williamson on editorial restructuring; kept the 'not_harmonized' label.
